claim: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that must precisely control their protein composition according to cellular energy demand.
source: Mitochondria are dynamic organelles that must precisely control their protein composition according to cellular energy demand.
evidence: This is a general statement about mitochondrial function that is established in the scientific literature.

claim: Nuclear-encoded mRNAs can be localized to the mitochondrial surface.
source: Although nuclear-encoded mRNAs can be localized to the mitochondrial surface, the importance of this localization is unclear.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and is a known phenomenon in the field.

claim: As yeast switch to respiratory metabolism, there is an increase in the fraction of the cytoplasm that is mitochondrial.
source: As yeast switch to respiratory metabolism, there is an increase in the fraction of the cytoplasm that is mitochondrial.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing increased mitochondrial volume fraction in respiratory conditions.

claim: The change in mitochondrial volume fraction increases the localization of certain nuclear-encoded mRNAs to the surface of the mitochondria.
source: Our data point to this change in mitochondrial volume fraction increasing the localization of certain nuclear-encoded mRNAs to the surface of the mitochondria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing correlation between mitochondrial volume fraction and mRNA localization.

claim: Mitochondrial mRNA localization is necessary and sufficient to increase protein production to levels required during respiratory growth.
source: We show that mitochondrial mRNA localization is necessary and sufficient to increase protein production to levels required during respiratory growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased protein production when mRNAs are tethered to mitochondria and decreased production when localization is prevented.

claim: Ribosome stalling impacts mRNA sensitivity to mitochondrial volume fraction.
source: Furthermore, we find that ribosome stalling impacts mRNA sensitivity to mitochondrial volume fraction and counterintuitively leads to enhanced protein synthesis by increasing mRNA localization to mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that insertion of polyproline sequences (which cause ribosome stalling) affects mRNA localization and protein synthesis.

claim: Ribosome stalling leads to enhanced protein synthesis by increasing mRNA localization to mitochondria.
source: Furthermore, we find that ribosome stalling impacts mRNA sensitivity to mitochondrial volume fraction and counterintuitively leads to enhanced protein synthesis by increasing mRNA localization to mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased protein production when polyproline sequences are inserted into ATP3.

claim: Mitochondria are essential cellular organelles that are key sources of ATP generation via oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Mitochondria are essential cellular organelles that are key sources of ATP generation via oxidative phosphorylation as well as the assembly of iron-sulfur clusters and many other catabolic and anabolic reactions (Attardi and Schatz, 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell biology supported by a citation.

claim: Proteins from hundreds of nuclear genes are imported into mitochondria from the cytoplasm.
source: To support mitochondrial function, proteins from hundreds of nuclear genes are imported into mitochondria from the cytoplasm (Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The mitochondrial genome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae contains 13 genes.
source: This has to be coordinated with the gene expression of the mitochondrial genome, which in Saccharomyces cerevisiae contains 13 genes (Borst and Grivell, 1978).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about yeast mitochondrial genome supported by a citation.

claim: S. cerevisiae are Crabtree-positive yeast and will actively repress respiration and the use of alternative carbon sources in conditions in which the fermentable carbon source glucose is present.
source: S. cerevisiae are Crabtree-positive yeast and will actively repress respiration and the use of alternative carbon sources in conditions in which the fermentable carbon source glucose is present (De Deken, 1966).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast metabolism supported by a citation.

claim: The yield of ATP per glucose molecule is much higher in respiration compared to fermentation.
source: This seems counterintuitive as the yield of ATP per glucose molecule is much higher in respiration compared to fermentation, but it is thought that fermentation allows higher fluxes of metabolite processing, leading to faster growth (van Dijken et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge in biochemistry supported by a citation.

claim: Fermentation allows higher fluxes of metabolite processing, leading to faster growth.
source: This seems counterintuitive as the yield of ATP per glucose molecule is much higher in respiration compared to fermentation, but it is thought that fermentation allows higher fluxes of metabolite processing, leading to faster growth (van Dijken et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents an explanation for the Crabtree effect.

claim: As cells run out of glucose they must switch their primary ATP generation source from fermentation to respiration.
source: Yet as cells run out of glucose they must switch their primary ATP generation source from fermentation to respiration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast metabolism.

claim: The metabolic change from fermentation to respiration is known to dramatically change the mitochondrial morphology.
source: This metabolic change is known to dramatically change the mitochondrial morphology (Egner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The protein content of yeast mitochondria shows dynamic changes in response to shifting cellular energy demands.
source: The protein content of yeast mitochondria also shows dynamic changes in response to shifting cellular energy demands (Morgenstern et al., 2017; Paulo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous proteomic studies.

claim: The HAP complex plays an important role in the transcriptional upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis upon a shift to non-fermentable carbon sources.
source: The HAP complex is known to play an important role in the transcriptional upregulation of mitochondrial biogenesis upon a shift to non-fermentable carbon sources (Buschlen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Translational regulation is important in the control of mitochondrial gene expression as oxidative phosphorylation protein coding mRNAs gradually increase their protein synthesis as the growth environment changes from fermentative growth to respiratory conditions.
source: Translational regulation has also been found to be important in the control of mitochondrial gene expression as oxidative phosphorylation protein coding mRNAs gradually increase their protein synthesis as the growth environment changes from fermentative growth to respiratory conditions (Couvillion et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In the 1970s, electron microscopy analysis found that cytoplasmic ribosomes can be localized along the mitochondrial outer membrane.
source: In the 1970s, electron microscopy analysis found that cytoplasmic ribosomes can be localized along the mitochondrial outer membrane (Kellems et al., 1974).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to historical work.

claim: Recent microarray and RNA-seq analyses of biochemically fractionated mitochondrial membranes and fluorescent microscopy analysis have identified subsets of nuclear-encoded mRNAs that are mitochondrially localized.
source: Recent microarray and RNA-seq analyses of biochemically fractionated mitochondrial membranes and fluorescent microscopy analysis have identified subsets of nuclear-encoded mRNAs that are mitochondrially localized (Fazal et al., 2019; Gadir et al., 2011; Garcia et al., 2007; Marc et al., 2002; Saint-Georges et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Both the 3′ UTR and coding regions, primarily through mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTSs), contribute to mitochondrial localization.
source: It has been shown that both the 3′ UTR and coding regions, primarily through mitochondrial targeting sequences (MTSs), contribute to mitochondrial localization.
evidence: This is supported by previous literature on mRNA localization mechanisms.

claim: One class of localized mRNAs (Class I) was shown to be dependent on the Puf3 RNA-binding protein through binding motifs in the 3′ UTR.
source: One class of localized mRNAs (Class I) was shown to be dependent on the Puf3 RNA-binging protein through binding motifs in the 3′ UTR (Saint-Georges et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Another class of mRNAs was localized to the mitochondria independently of Puf3 (Class II).
source: Another class of mRNAs was localized to the mitochondria independently of Puf3 (Class II).
evidence: This is supported by previous literature on mRNA localization.

claim: Many of the localized mRNAs show reduced association upon polysome dissociation through EDTA or puromycin treatment, implicating translation as a necessary factor for mRNA localization.
source: Many of the localized mRNAs show reduced association upon polysome dissociation through EDTA or puromycin treatment, implicating translation as a necessary factor for mRNA localization (Eliyahu et al., 2010; Fazal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The mitochondrial translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex has been shown to impact mRNA localization through interaction with the nascent MTS.
source: The mitochondrial translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex has been shown to impact mRNA localization through interaction with the nascent MTS (Eliyahu et al., 2010), while the outer-membrane protein OM14 has been shown to be a mitochondrial receptor for the ribosome nascent-chain-associated complex (NAC) (Lesnik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The outer-membrane protein OM14 has been shown to be a mitochondrial receptor for the ribosome nascent-chain-associated complex (NAC).
source: The mitochondrial translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) complex has been shown to impact mRNA localization through interaction with the nascent MTS (Eliyahu et al., 2010), while the outer-membrane protein OM14 has been shown to be a mitochondrial receptor for the ribosome nascent-chain-associated complex (NAC) (Lesnik et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Isolating mitochondrially localized ribosomes to perform proximity-specific ribosome profiling revealed that many mitochondrial inner-membrane protein mRNAs are co-translationally targeted to the mitochondria.
source: Isolating mitochondrially localized ribosomes to perform proximity-specific ribosome profiling revealed that many mitochondrial inner-membrane protein mRNAs are co-translationally targeted to the mitochondria (Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TIM50 mRNA is strongly associated with the mitochondria during fermentative growth.
source: During fermentative growth, we observed TIM50 mRNA to be strongly associated with the mitochondria, whereas TOM22 showed low association consistent with previous studies (Figure 1B; Video 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TOM22 showed low association with mitochondria during fermentative growth, consistent with previous studies.
source: During fermentative growth, we observed TIM50 mRNA to be strongly associated with the mitochondria, whereas TOM22 showed low association consistent with previous studies (Figure 1B; Video 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: ATP3 has low association with mitochondria, similar to TOM22, in fermentative conditions.
source: Even though ATP3 had previously been categorized as a mitochondrially localized mRNA (Gadir et al., 2011; Saint-Georges et al., 2008), we unexpectedly found this to be condition-dependent as it has low association with mitochondria, similar to TOM22, in fermentative conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and contrasts with previous literature.

claim: ATP3 mRNA strongly shifts towards association with the mitochondrial surface during respiratory conditions.
source: However, during respiratory conditions it strongly shifted towards association with the mitochondrial surface, in a manner more similar to TIM50 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs can show a switch-like behavior depending on the metabolic state of the cell.
source: This means that nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs do not have to be solely mitochondrially localized or diffusely localized; instead, they can show a switch-like behavior depending on the metabolic state of the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing condition-dependent localization of ATP3 mRNA.

claim: For ATP3 mRNA, protein levels increased 4-fold when cells were grown in respiratory versus fermentative conditions.
source: For the condition-dependent ATP3 mRNA, we found that protein levels increased 4-fold, whereas mRNA levels increased less than 2-fold when cells were grown in respiratory versus fermentative conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: For ATP3 mRNA, mRNA levels increased less than 2-fold when cells were grown in respiratory versus fermentative conditions.
source: For the condition-dependent ATP3 mRNA, we found that protein levels increased 4-fold, whereas mRNA levels increased less than 2-fold when cells were grown in respiratory versus fermentative conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TIM50 mRNA showed no change in protein or mRNA levels in respiratory conditions.
source: TIM50 mRNA, which is constitutively localized to the mitochondria under both conditions, showed no change in protein or mRNA levels in respiratory conditions (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: There is a relationship between mRNA localization to the mitochondria and protein production.
source: This suggests a relationship between mRNA localization to the mitochondria and protein production.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that ATP3 mRNA localization increases in respiratory conditions along with increased protein production.

claim: As yeast cells shift to respiratory conditions, mitochondrial biogenesis increases the mitochondrial volume while the cell cytoplasmic volume decreases, leading to an increase in the mitochondrial volume fraction.
source: As yeast cells shift to respiratory conditions, mitochondrial biogenesis increases the mitochondrial volume while the cell cytoplasmic volume decreases, thus leading to an increase in the mitochondrial volume fraction in respiratory conditions (Egner et al., 2002; Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, as well as a citation.

claim: TOM22 showed a linear increase in co-localization that was directly proportional to mitochondrial volume fraction.
source: We found that TOM22 showed a linear increase in co-localization that was directly proportional to mitochondrial volume fraction (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ATP3 mRNA was more sensitive to mitochondrial volume fraction than TIM50 and TOM22.
source: We also found that ATP3 mRNA was more sensitive to mitochondrial volume fraction than TIM50 and TOM22.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The sensitivity of ATP3 mRNA to mitochondrial volume fraction was independent of nutrients, as fermentative yeast cells showed a larger increase in ATP3 localization as the mitochondrial volume fraction increased.
source: This sensitivity was independent of nutrients, as fermentative yeast cells showed a larger increase in ATP3 localization as the mitochondrial volume fraction increased (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At the lowest mitochondrial volume fractions, ATP3 localization was similar to the diffusely localized TOM22 mRNA.
source: At the lowest mitochondrial volume fractions, ATP3 localization was similar to the diffusely localized TOM22 mRNA, whereas at the highest volume fractions, its localization was close to the mitochondrially localized mRNA TIM50.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At the highest mitochondrial volume fractions, ATP3 localization was close to the mitochondrially localized mRNA TIM50.
source: At the lowest mitochondrial volume fractions, ATP3 localization was similar to the diffusely localized TOM22 mRNA, whereas at the highest volume fractions, its localization was close to the mitochondrially localized mRNA TIM50.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased mitochondrial volume fraction increases ATP3 mRNA localization to mitochondria.
source: This suggests that increased mitochondrial volume fraction in turn increases ATP3 mRNA localization to mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing correlation between mitochondrial volume fraction and ATP3 mRNA localization.

claim: In glucose conditions, sch9∆ and reg1∆ mutant strains as well as chloramphenicol addition exhibit higher mitochondrial volume fraction and increase the localization of ATP3 mRNA to the mitochondria.
source: In glucose conditions, sch9∆ and reg1∆ mutant strains as well as chloramphenicol addition exhibit higher mitochondrial volume fraction and increase the localization of ATP3 mRNA to the mitochondria (n > 27).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: reg1∆ cells exhibit increased mitochondrial function in glucose media.
source: Reg1 is a protein necessary for glucose repression in yeast, and reg1∆ cells exhibit increased mitochondrial function in glucose media (Adachi et al., 2017; Hübscher et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chloramphenicol decreases mitochondrial protein synthesis while having no effect on cytoplasmic translation.
source: Additionally, the antibiotic chloramphenicol is known to decrease mitochondrial protein synthesis while having no effect on cytoplasmic translation and has been found to increase the fraction of mitochondrial protein in Neurospora crassa and mitochondrial volume in Tetrahymena pyriformis (Brody, 1992; Gleason et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Chloramphenicol has been found to increase the fraction of mitochondrial protein in Neurospora crassa and mitochondrial volume in Tetrahymena pyriformis.
source: Additionally, the antibiotic chloramphenicol is known to decrease mitochondrial protein synthesis while having no effect on cytoplasmic translation and has been found to increase the fraction of mitochondrial protein in Neurospora crassa and mitochondrial volume in Tetrahymena pyriformis (Brody, 1992; Gleason et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeast cells treated with chloramphenicol showed an ~70% increase in mitochondria volume fraction.
source: We observed an ~70% increase in mitochondria volume fraction in yeast cells treated with chloramphenicol and, simultaneously, a ~ 50% increase in ATP3 mRNA mitochondrial association during vegetative conditions (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplements 3A–D and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: Yeast cells treated with chloramphenicol showed a ~50% increase in ATP3 mRNA mitochondrial association during vegetative conditions.
source: We observed an ~70% increase in mitochondria volume fraction in yeast cells treated with chloramphenicol and, simultaneously, a ~ 50% increase in ATP3 mRNA mitochondrial association during vegetative conditions (Figure 2E; Figure 2—figure supplements 3A–D and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: Mitochondrial volume fraction is the important variable for ATP3 mRNA localization and not a factor related to respiration.
source: These results support the hypothesis that mitochondrial volume fraction is the important variable for ATP3 mRNA localization and not a factor related to respiration, as chloramphenicol decreases respiratory function (Williamson et al., 1971) while increasing mitochondrial volume fraction and ATP3 localization.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that chloramphenicol, which inhibits respiration, still increases ATP3 localization when it increases mitochondrial volume fraction.

claim: sch9∆ was previously found to be one of the smallest strains from a genome-wide screen for cell size.
source: sch9∆ was previously found to be one of the smallest strains from a genome-wide screen for cell size (Jorgensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ATP3 mRNAs showed increased mitochondrial association in sch9∆.
source: We found that ATP3 mRNAs showed increased mitochondrial association in sch9∆, though from initial analysis this was not accompanied by an increase in mitochondrial volume fraction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: The vacuole volume fraction was ~6 x higher in sch9∆ cells versus WT cells.
source: While imaging these cells, we noticed a large increase in the relative vacuole in sch9∆ cells; the vacuole volume fraction was ~6 x higher in sch9∆ cells versus WT cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3F.

claim: sch9∆ cells have a significant increase in mitochondrial volume fraction after correcting for vacuole volume.
source: As the vacuole restricts the accessible cytoplasmic volume, we recalculated the mitochondrial volume fraction relative to the accessible cytosol and found that sch9∆ cells have a significant increase in mitochondrial volume fraction after this correction (Figure 2—figure supplements 3E–F and 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 3E-F.

claim: The relationship between mitochondrial volume fraction and mRNA localization holds across highly varied perturbations, including nutritional (glucose/glycerol), genetic (reg1∆, sch9∆), and pharmacological (chloramphenicol).
source: These results show that the relationship between mitochondrial volume fraction and mRNA localization holds across highly varied perturbations, including nutritional (glucose/glycerol), genetic (reg1∆, sch9∆), and pharmacological (chloramphenicol).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from multiple perturbations shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: Most potential receptors, including the import machinery, TOM/SAM complex, do not show a difference in expression between respiratory and fermentative conditions.
source: Surprisingly, most of these potential receptors, including the import machinery, TOM/SAM complex, do not show a difference in expression between respiratory and fermentative conditions (Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published proteomics data.

claim: The outer membrane receptors OM14 and OM45 had a significant 7 to 9-fold increase in expression when mitochondrial volume fraction is expanded.
source: The outer membrane receptors OM14 and OM45 did have a significant 7 to 9-fold increase in expression when mitochondrial volume fraction is expanded.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published proteomics data.

claim: There is no significant increase in the expression of OM14 and OM45 RNAs in reg1∆ and sch9∆ mutant strains.
source: While we are able to recapitulate the large increase in expression of OM14 and OM45 in respiratory conditions, we do not find a significant increase in the expression of these RNAs in reg1∆ and sch9∆ mutant strains (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The TIM50 MTS is necessary to recruit this mRNA to mitochondria.
source: Even though TIM50 mRNA was associated with mitochondria, ER-TIM50, TOM22, ER-TOM22, and TIM50-∆MTS mRNAs were not associated with mitochondria (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that the TIM50 MTS is necessary to recruit this mRNA to mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TIM50 mRNA in all conditions and ATP3 mRNA in respiratory conditions decreased localization to the mitochondrial surface upon lactimidomycin (LTM) addition.
source: We found that TIM50 mRNA in all conditions and ATP3 mRNA in respiratory conditions decreased localization to the mitochondrial surface upon LTM addition, while ATP3 mRNA in fermentative conditions showed only minimal changes in localization upon LTM addition (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ATP3 mRNA in fermentative conditions showed only minimal changes in localization upon LTM addition.
source: We found that TIM50 mRNA in all conditions and ATP3 mRNA in respiratory conditions decreased localization to the mitochondrial surface upon LTM addition, while ATP3 mRNA in fermentative conditions showed only minimal changes in localization upon LTM addition (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The actively translating ribosome drives mRNA localization to mitochondria through production of the nascent N-terminal MTS.
source: These results suggest that the actively translating ribosome drives mRNA localization to mitochondria through production of the nascent N-terminal MTS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that translation inhibition reduces mRNA localization.

claim: When the reporter gene contained the TIM50-CDS, it showed uniform protein production in fermentative versus respiratory conditions, independent of which MTS was present.
source: When the reporter gene contained the TIM50-CDS, it showed uniform protein production in fermentative versus respiratory conditions, independent of which MTS was present (Figure 3C, lane 1 vs. 2 and lane 5 vs. 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When the reporter gene contained the ATP3-CDS, it showed decreased protein production in fermentative conditions.
source: However, when the reporter gene contained the ATP3-CDS, it showed decreased protein production in fermentative conditions (Figure 3C, lane 3 vs. 4 and lane 7 vs. 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The reporter genes that harbored the ATP3-CDS showed decreased proportion of mitochondrial associated mRNA in fermentative but not in respiratory conditions.
source: Similarly, the reporter genes that harbored the ATP3-CDS also showed decreased proportion of mitochondrial associated mRNA in fermentative but not in respiratory conditions (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The TIM50 and ATP3 MTS have similar affinities for the mitochondria.
source: These experiments suggest that the TIM50 and ATP3 MTS have similar affinities for the mitochondria and, importantly, what drives the condition-specific differences in mRNA localization and protein production between these mRNAs is encoded in the downstream CDS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that swapping MTSs does not change the localization behavior.

claim: What drives the condition-specific differences in mRNA localization and protein production between TIM50 and ATP3 mRNAs is encoded in the downstream CDS.
source: These experiments suggest that the TIM50 and ATP3 MTS have similar affinities for the mitochondria and, importantly, what drives the condition-specific differences in mRNA localization and protein production between these mRNAs is encoded in the downstream CDS.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that the CDS determines localization behavior.

claim: The TIM50 CDS has a run of 7 consecutive proline codons approximately 60 amino acids downstream of the MTS.
source: Upon further examination, we found that the TIM50 CDS has a run of 7 consecutive proline codons approximately 60 amino acids downstream of the MTS.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of the TIM50 gene.

claim: Polyproline stretches have been shown to mediate ribosome stalling.
source: Polyproline stretches have been shown to mediate ribosome stalling, and, when we investigated a ribosome profiling data set, we found that ribosomes accumulate at this polyproline stretch during fermentative conditions (Zid and O'Shea, 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ribosomes accumulate at the polyproline stretch in TIM50 during fermentative conditions.
source: Polyproline stretches have been shown to mediate ribosome stalling, and, when we investigated a ribosome profiling data set, we found that ribosomes accumulate at this polyproline stretch during fermentative conditions (Zid and O'Shea, 2014; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deleting the polyproline residues from TIM50 caused it to be more sensitive to environmental conditions as it reduced both protein synthesis and mRNA localization of TIM50 during fermentative conditions.
source: To test this, we deleted these polyproline residues and found this caused TIM50 to be more sensitive to environmental conditions as it reduced both protein synthesis and mRNA localization of TIM50 during fermentative conditions (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Inserting a run of 7 consecutive proline codons at 100 amino acids downstream of the start codon in ATP3 increased protein production 1.6-fold in fermentative conditions.
source: To test this hypothesis, we inserted a run of 7 consecutive proline codons at 100 amino acids downstream of the start codon and analyzed protein expression in fermentative conditions (Figure 4A, right). We observed that protein production is increased 1.6-fold (Figure 4E) and mRNA localization is increased as well (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Inserting a run of 7 consecutive proline codons at 100 amino acids downstream of the start codon in ATP3 increased mRNA localization in fermentative conditions.
source: To test this hypothesis, we inserted a run of 7 consecutive proline codons at 100 amino acids downstream of the start codon and analyzed protein expression in fermentative conditions (Figure 4A, right). We observed that protein production is increased 1.6-fold (Figure 4E) and mRNA localization is increased as well (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ribosome stalling leads to mRNA localization to mitochondria and increased protein production.
source: Overall these results further suggest that ribosome stalling leads to mRNA localization to mitochondria and increased protein production.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that polyproline insertion increases both localization and protein production.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment caused a 3-fold increase in the association of ATP3 mRNA with mitochondria during fermentative conditions.
source: As our hypothesis predicted, we observed a 3-fold increase in the association of ATP3 mRNA with mitochondria during fermentative conditions but no increase in the case of TOM22 mRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment did not increase the association of TOM22 mRNA with mitochondria.
source: As our hypothesis predicted, we observed a 3-fold increase in the association of ATP3 mRNA with mitochondria during fermentative conditions but no increase in the case of TOM22 mRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CHX treatment only slightly increased TIM50 mRNA localization.
source: Interestingly, CHX treatment only slightly increased TIM50 mRNA localization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 130 of 551 annotated nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs are sensitive to translation elongation rate and become localized to the mitochondrial surface upon cycloheximide treatment, similar to ATP3.
source: A previous study found that 130 of 551 annotated nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs are sensitive to translation elongation rate and become localized to the mitochondrial surface upon cycloheximide treatment, similar to ATP3 (Figure 5B; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All of the ATP synthase subunits that are conserved from bacteria to eukaryotes are sensitive to cycloheximide, except for the ε subunit, ATP16.
source: Interestingly, all of the ATP synthase subunits that are conserved from bacteria to eukaryotes are sensitive to cycloheximide, except for the ε subunit, ATP16, whereas all of the nonconserved subunits are insensitive to cycloheximide (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of previous data shown in Table 1.

claim: All of the nonconserved ATP synthase subunits are insensitive to cycloheximide.
source: Interestingly, all of the ATP synthase subunits that are conserved from bacteria to eukaryotes are sensitive to cycloheximide, except for the ε subunit, ATP16, whereas all of the nonconserved subunits are insensitive to cycloheximide (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of previous data shown in Table 1.

claim: ATP2 showed a large increase in localization according to volume fraction change upon a shift to respiratory conditions and was sensitive to cycloheximide.
source: We tested ATP2, the conserved β subunit of the ATP synthase, and found that it was similar to ATP3 in that it showed a large increase in localization according to volume fraction change upon a shift to respiratory conditions and was sensitive to cycloheximide (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATP7 behaved more like TOM22 in that it was insensitive to cycloheximide and had a much smaller increase in mitochondrial localization in respiratory conditions than ATP2 or ATP3.
source: However, the nonconserved subunit, ATP7, behaved more like TOM22 in that it was insensitive to cycloheximide and had a much smaller increase in mitochondrial localization in respiratory conditions than ATP2 or ATP3 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ATP3-type mRNAs had a significant increase in their protein productive capacity versus TIM50-type as they had >2 fold more ribosomes engaged in translation in the shift from glucose to glycerol.
source: From this data, we found that ATP3-type mRNAs had a significant increase in their protein productive capacity versus TIM50-type as they had >2 fold more ribosomes engaged in translation in the shift from glucose to glycerol (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The increase in protein production for ATP3-type mRNAs was caused by both a significant increase in translation efficiency and mRNA levels during respiratory conditions.
source: The increase in protein production was caused by both a significant increase in translation efficiency and mRNA levels for ATP3-type mRNAs during respiratory conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ATP3-type genes had an increase in protein abundance during respiratory conditions versus TIM50-type genes.
source: From an independent proteomics data set under glucose and glycerol conditions, we also found that ATP3-type genes had an increase in protein abundance during respiratory conditions versus TIM50-type genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C; Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published proteomics data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Tethering TIM50-flag-GFP-12xMS2 and ATP3-flag-GFP-12xMS2 mRNA to the mitochondria was sufficient to upregulate protein production.
source: We found that tethering TIM50-flag-GFP-12xMS2 and ATP3-flag-GFP-12xMS2 mRNA to the mitochondria was sufficient to upregulate protein production.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Protein production was increased independent of the mRNA harboring an MTS, as an mRNA that contained flag-GFP with no mitochondrial coding sequences also showed increased protein production when tethered to mitochondria.
source: Surprisingly, protein production was increased independent of the mRNA harboring an MTS, as an mRNA that contained flag-GFP with no mitochondrial coding sequences also showed increased protein production (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Increased protein expression was observed when mRNA was tethered to the ER.
source: We also saw increased protein production when mRNA was tethered to the ER, suggesting that the surface of both of these organelles may harbor the capacity for enhanced protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Increased mRNA levels were observed when mRNAs were tethered to the mitochondria.
source: In addition to increased protein expression, we also observed increased mRNA levels when mRNAs were tethered to the mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The ratio of protein to mRNA was much higher when mRNAs were tethered to the mitochondria.
source: However, the ratio of protein to mRNA was much higher (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A 3-fold increase in ribosome association rate was observed from sucrose density fractionated mRNAs for mRNAs that were tethered to the mitochondria.
source: We further observed a 3-fold increase in ribosome association rate from sucrose density fractionated mRNAs for mRNAs that were tethered to the mitochondria (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that translational efficiency is increased on the mitochondrial surface.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Translational efficiency is increased on the mitochondrial surface.
source: We further observed a 3-fold increase in ribosome association rate from sucrose density fractionated mRNAs for mRNAs that were tethered to the mitochondria (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), suggesting that translational efficiency is increased on the mitochondrial surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased ribosome association when mRNAs are tethered to mitochondria.

claim: Directing ATP3 and TIM50 mRNAs to the plasma membrane caused a decrease in protein reporter levels during respiratory conditions.
source: To test whether localization to the mitochondria is necessary for optimal protein production during respiratory conditions, we reduced the localization of endogenous ATP3 and TIM50 mRNA to mitochondria by directing those mRNAs to the plasma membrane via insertion of a CaaX-tag to the C termini of MCP-GFP proteins during respiratory conditions (Yan et al., 2016). This caused a decrease in protein reporter levels of mitochondrial localized mRNAs, such as TIM50, ATP3, and ATP2, but not in non-mitochondrially localized mRNAs, such as TOM22 and GFP alone (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells in which ATP3 mRNA was anchored to the plasma membrane and away from the mitochondria in respiratory conditions showed a growth defect.
source: We next investigated whether enhancing protein synthesis was essential for optimal cell growth. Cells in which ATP3 mRNA was anchored to the plasma membrane and away from the mitochondria in respiratory conditions showed a growth defect, whereas ER tethering of mRNAs, which does not impair protein synthesis, did not affect cell growth (Figure 6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: ER tethering of mRNAs, which does not impair protein synthesis, did not affect cell growth.
source: We next investigated whether enhancing protein synthesis was essential for optimal cell growth. Cells in which ATP3 mRNA was anchored to the plasma membrane and away from the mitochondria in respiratory conditions showed a growth defect, whereas ER tethering of mRNAs, which does not impair protein synthesis, did not affect cell growth (Figure 6G; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Localization of mRNA to mitochondria is important for optimal cell growth because it drives enhanced protein synthesis during respiratory conditions.
source: This suggests that localization of mRNA to mitochondria is important for optimal cell growth because it drives enhanced protein synthesis during respiratory conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that preventing mitochondrial localization causes a growth defect.

claim: Yeast cells can use the geometric constraints that arise from increased mitochondrial volume fraction during respiratory conditions to increase condition-dependent mitochondrial localization for a subset of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs.
source: We demonstrate that yeast cells can use the geometric constraints that arise from increased mitochondrial volume fraction during respiratory conditions to increase condition-dependent mitochondrial localization for a subset of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial mRNAs.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The simple mathematical model incorporating mitochondrial volume fraction and various binding affinities is able to recapitulate the mRNA localization effects seen in cells.
source: We favor the hypothesis that the geometric constraints of mitochondrial volume fraction are an important factor impacting mRNA localization for two reasons: first, our simple mathematical model incorporating mitochondrial volume fraction and various binding affinities is able to recapitulate the mRNA localization effects we see in cells.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Translation duration plays an important role in mRNA localization to the mitochondria.
source: Our results also indicate that translation duration plays an important role in mRNA localization to the mitochondria.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that ribosome stalling affects mRNA localization.

claim: Translation duration and mitochondrial volume fraction are interconnected, as both will impact the probability of the mitochondria interacting with a competent mRNA.
source: We believe that translation duration and mitochondrial volume fraction are interconnected, as both will impact the probability of the mitochondria interacting with a competent mRNA, meaning the MTS is exposed while still attached to the mRNA as a nascent-polypeptide (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: ATP3 mRNA, which has fast translation elongation compared to TIM50, is in a competent state for a shorter period of time, so during fermentative conditions it is less likely to interact with mitochondria while in a competent state.
source: ATP3 mRNA, which has fast translation elongation compared to TIM50, is in a competent state for a shorter period of time, so during fermentative conditions it is less likely to interact with mitochondria while in a competent state (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data shown in the model in Figure 7B.

claim: Ribosome stalling along TIM50 mRNA prolongs the time the mRNA is in a competent state, and this increases its probability of interacting with mitochondria even when in low mitochondrial volume fraction conditions.
source: Conversely, ribosome stalling along TIM50 mRNA prolongs the time the mRNA is in a competent state, and this increases its probability of interacting with mitochondria even when in low mitochondrial volume fraction conditions (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data shown in the model in Figure 7B.

claim: As the mitochondrial volume fraction of cells increases as they shift to respiratory conditions, there is a higher probability of competent mRNAs interacting with the mitochondria, even if they are only competent for a short time.
source: As the mitochondrial volume fraction of cells increases as they shift to respiratory conditions, there is a higher probability of competent mRNAs interacting with the mitochondria, even if they are only competent for a short time (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the experimental data shown in the model in Figure 7B.

claim: The localization of ribosomes on the yeast mitochondrial surface has been known since the 1970s, implicating localized translation.
source: The localization of ribosomes on the yeast mitochondrial surface has been known since the 1970 s, implicating localized translation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by historical citations.

claim: mRNA localization to mitochondria has an alternative function: to upregulate protein synthesis.
source: Our work points to localization to mitochondria having an alternative function: to upregulate protein synthesis, as we found that mRNA localization to mitochondria was sufficient to increase protein synthesis, whereas tethering mRNAs away from the mitochondria to the plasma membrane reduced protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The decrease in protein levels when ATP3 mRNA is anchored to the plasma membrane is associated with a growth defect during respiratory conditions.
source: The decrease in protein levels when ATP3 mRNA is anchored to the plasma membrane is also associated with a growth defect during respiratory conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: When ATP3 mRNAs were targeted away from the mitochondria to the ER, there was no growth defect.
source: Yet localization to the mitochondria is not absolutely required for optimal growth; when ATP3 mRNAs were targeted away from the mitochondria to the ER, there was no growth defect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Similar to the mitochondria, there is an upregulation of protein levels when mRNAs are targeted to the ER.
source: This may be because, similar to the mitochondria, there is an upregulation of protein levels when mRNAs are targeted to the ER.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: Condition-dependent mRNA localization to the mitochondria as a means to control gene expression could be used to tune the protein composition of the mitochondria to the metabolic needs of the cell.
source: Condition-dependent mRNA localization to the mitochondria as a means to control gene expression could be used to tune the protein composition of the mitochondria to the metabolic needs of the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: The conserved subunits of ATP synthase are all sensitive to the translation elongation rates in the cell, and these subunits showed similar localization regulation patterns.
source: For example, the conserved subunits of ATP synthase are all sensitive to the translation elongation rates in the cell, and these subunits showed similar localization regulation patterns (Table 1); this suggests that a mechanism may have evolved that coordinates the expression and stoichiometry of vital subunits of this complex.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of data shown in Table 1.

claim: Nuclear-encoded components of the F1 ATP synthase complex upregulate the translation of the mitochondrially encoded ATP6 and ATP8 subunits potentially contributing to the synchronization of these separated genomes.
source: Interestingly it has been shown that nuclear-encoded components of the F1 ATP synthase complex upregulate the translation of the mitochondrially encoded ATP6 and ATP8 subunits potentially contributing to the synchronization of these separated genomes (Rak and Tzagoloff, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cycloheximide-sensitive mRNAs (ATP3-type) show a more than 2-fold increase in protein synthesis relative to constitutively localized mRNAs (TIM50-type) when cells shift from fermentation to respiration.
source: Further supporting the use of condition-dependent mRNA localization in impacting gene expression is global data showing that cycloheximide-sensitive mRNAs (ATP3-type) show a more than 2-fold increase in protein synthesis relative to constitutively localized mRNAs (TIM50-type) when cells shift from fermentation to respiration (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: For ATP3-type mRNAs, the increase in protein synthesis during respiratory conditions is driven by both increases in translational efficiency and increased mRNA levels.
source: For ATP3-type mRNAs, the increase in protein synthesis during respiratory conditions is driven by both increases in translational efficiency and increased mRNA levels (Figure 1C–E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The increase in protein levels seen when mRNAs were tethered to the mitochondria was driven by both an increase in mRNA levels and ribosome engagement.
source: Similarly, the increase in protein levels seen when mRNAs were tethered to the mitochondria was driven by both an increase in mRNA levels and ribosome engagement (Figure 6C–E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Localization to the mitochondria increases mRNA stability.
source: As these reporter mRNAs are under identical promoters, we favor the hypothesis that localization to the mitochondria increases mRNA stability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that tethered mRNAs have increased levels despite being under the same promoter.

claim: Increased translation initiation can lead to protection from mRNA degradation.
source: It is unclear whether translational efficiency and mRNA stability are independently affected by localization to the mitochondria or whether they are interrelated, as previous reports have shown that increased translation initiation can lead to protection from mRNA degradation (Roy and Jacobson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ribosome stalling increases mRNA binding competency, driving mRNA localization to the mitochondria, along with increased translation initiation and mRNA stability.
source: As discussed previously, ribosome stalling increases mRNA binding competency, driving mRNA localization to the mitochondria, along with increased translation initiation and mRNA stability.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Translation initiation is thought to be the rate-limiting step in translation for most mRNAs.
source: As translation initiation is thought to be the rate-limiting step in translation for most mRNAs, this would explain our somewhat-contradictory results showing that more ribosome stalling, through polyproline insertion, leads to increased protein synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of translation.

claim: There may be an increased density of ribosomes on the mitochondrial surface.
source: We consider the simplest explanation, that there may be an increased density of ribosomes on the mitochondrial surface, as previously suggested in Drosophila oogenesis (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous work in a different organism.

claim: Translation initiation factors or mRNA decay factors may have altered activities near mitochondria that produce high levels of ATP.
source: It also might be true that translation initiation factors or mRNA decay factors have altered activities near mitochondria that produce high levels of ATP.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how mitochondrial localization might increase protein synthesis.

claim: There may be specialized ribosomes, enriched at the mitochondrial surface, that enhance translation.
source: An alternative idea is that there are specialized ribosomes, enriched at the mitochondrial surface, that enhance translation (Xue and Barna, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous work on specialized ribosomes.

claim: Specific ribosomal protein paralogs are necessary for normal mitochondrial function.
source: Intriguingly, it was recently found that specific ribosomal protein paralogs are necessary for normal mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Rpl1b∆ cells were found to be deficient for growth on nonfermentable carbon sources, whereas rpl1a∆ had no growth defect in these conditions.
source: Rpl1b∆ cells were found to be deficient for growth on nonfermentable carbon sources, whereas rpl1a∆ had no growth defect in these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: rpl1b∆ cells were found to have decreased translation of many mitochondrial proteins during respiratory conditions, including the ATP3-type mRNAs ATP1 and ATP2.
source: Furthermore, rpl1b∆ cells were found to have decreased translation of many mitochondrial proteins during respiratory conditions, including the ATP3-type mRNAs ATP1 and ATP2 (Segev and Gerst, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Higher eukaryotic cells could also use mitochondrial mRNA localization, controlled by translation elongation and mitochondrial volume fraction, to regulate protein synthesis.
source: While we have found this gene expression control mechanism in yeast, we speculate that higher eukaryotic cells could also use mitochondrial mRNA localization, controlled by translation elongation and mitochondrial volume fraction, to regulate protein synthesis.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: A recent paper exploring global mRNA localization in mammalian cells found that many ATP synthase mRNAs had enhanced localization to the mitochondria in a cycloheximide-dependent manner, similar to ATP3-type mRNAs in yeast.
source: Hinting at this, a recent paper exploring global mRNA localization in mammalian cells found that many ATP synthase mRNAs had enhanced localization to the mitochondria in a cycloheximide-dependent manner, similar to ATP3-type mRNAs in yeast (Fazal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent work in mammalian cells.

claim: More than 84% of the ORFs and MS2 sequences are a continuous stretch in the same mRNA.
source: Analysing the co-localization rate of candidate mRNA ORF and MS2 sequences using anti-sense probes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), we confirmed that more than 84% of the ORFs and MS2 sequences are a continuous stretch in the same mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The number of MCP-GFP foci in live cells is statistically no different than the number of smFISH foci in the tested mRNAs.
source: The number of MCP-GFP foci in live cells is statistically no different (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p-value<0.05, N > 43) than the number of smFISH foci in the tested mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The MCP-GFP foci in the live cell images are reliable single molecule mRNAs and not degradation intermediates.
source: We concluded that the MCP-GFP foci in the live cell images are reliable single molecule mRNAs and not degradation intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation experiments comparing live imaging to smFISH.
